chapter_title: The Chapter of the Nazorean who questions the Teac

spiritual_reading.full_translation:
Discernment that proceeds from the Divine is not wickedness; it is the effect of order resisting wickedness, restraining it, and setting bounds to its action. Yet to the outward view that same effect is spoken of as if it goes forth to punish and destroy, because it removes what is contrary to good and truth, brings its activity to an end, and so annuls evil and blocks its power within the person, turning it back upon its own source and fixing it as the person’s own guilt.

Still, the Divine does nothing evil to anyone; they do it to themselves. Their own chosen acts condemn them, and those acts carry them into the tormenting intensity of evil love and its consuming unrest.

paragraph_translations.translation: Discernment that proceeds from the Divine is not wickedness; it is the effect of order resisting wickedness, restraining it, and setting bounds to its action. Yet to the outward view that same effect is spoken of as if it goes forth to punish and destroy, because it removes what is contrary to good and truth, brings its activity to an end, and so annuls evil and blocks its power within the person, turning it back upon its own source and fixing it as the person’s own guilt.
paragraph_translations.connection: DEVELOPS the teaching by clarifying that apparent punishment is the operation of order restraining evil and returning it upon its origin.
paragraph_translations.notes: “Judge” translates cleanly as Divine discernment operating as order. The piling of punitive verbs forces a single spiritual action described in varied outward terms.

paragraph_translations.translation: Still, the Divine does nothing evil to anyone; they do it to themselves. Their own chosen acts condemn them, and those acts carry them into the tormenting intensity of evil love and its consuming unrest.
paragraph_translations.connection: CONTINUES by shifting the blame from the Divine to the self-chosen acts that bring a person into their own torment.
paragraph_translations.notes: “Gehenna of burning” required a translation into the felt state of infernal love and its torment; the imagery is consistent and yields coherent spiritual sense.

spiritual_reading.overall_coherence: High coherence: both paragraphs speak in one voice about the same law of order—Divine discernment is perceived as punitive when it restrains and ends evil, and condemnation is self-induced through chosen acts. The movement from appearance (punishment) to cause (self-choice) is smooth and unified.

findings.diagnosis: Coherent correspondential teaching: “judge/punish” language is explained as the function of order limiting evil, not as a jurisdictional or mythic administration. No seam, no list, no named powers. The paragraph’s internal logic resolves the apparent contradiction (“judge” yet “not wicked”).
findings.evidence: Text: “The judge is not a man of wickedness, but rather the work counteracts wickedness, limiting the evil… He acts like this that he might annul the evil and impede the wickedness in the person; and lay it upon the head of the sinner.” This is functional/operational: the ‘judge’ is defined by what happens (counteracting, limiting, annulling, impeding). Stage 3a explicitly reports no stumble: “Judge translates cleanly as Divine discernment operating as order… the punitive verbs force a single spiritual action described in varied outward terms.” That is exactly what a clean correspondential substrate looks like: outward punitive predicates re-read as one inward action of restraint and consequence.

findings.diagnosis: Coherent continuation in the same correspondential voice: the causal account (“they do it to themselves”) keeps the narrative line and explains ‘gehenna’ as the experiential outcome of chosen deeds. No administrative overlay markers (no ranks, stations, rulers, inventories).
findings.evidence: Text: “God has not done anything that is ev[il to] them, rather they to themselves. It is their own deeds that shall condemn them and cast them in the gehenna of burning.” The logic is causal and moral-psychological (deeds → condemnation → experienced burning), not governmental. The spiritual reading notes a minor interpretive step (“Gehenna of burning required a translation into the felt state…”) but explicitly says “the imagery is consistent and yields coherent spiritual sense,” and “the movement… is smooth and unified.” There is no narrative break that would improve by omission.

findings.diagnosis: No detectable voice-boundary seam or Mani-style administrative expansion. The chapter is very short (likely excerpted), but what survives is internally consistent and reads like a single teaching unit.
findings.evidence: Across both paragraphs the teaching stays on one axis: apparent divine punishment is the operation of order restraining evil; condemnation is self-incurred. Stage 3a’s “Overall coherence: High coherence… one voice… smooth and unified” indicates the reader did not have to force harmonization or explain away alien material—typical signs of later administrative insertion are absent (named authorities, territorial assignments, fivefold inventories, bridge connectives introducing new systems).

textual_criticism.summary: 0 issues found. All surviving paragraphs (¶6, ¶11) read in a unified correspondential voice, and the spiritual reading reports no narrative stumble. No excisions or administrative-block annotations are warranted on the present evidence; the only limitation is the fragmentary/abridged chapter extent, not textual disruption.
